\section*{Score-I papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Degrees of freedom}, answer={16}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: temperature or pressure after oxygen dissociation, a gas mixture | steps: moles of CO2; atoms of O formed double the O2 moles; ideal gas pressure changes; first law energy for dissociation; solve | I: dissociation changes number of moles}]
A mixture of some $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 22 g $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is subjected to some change such that all the $\mathrm{O_2}$ molecules dissociated into atoms. The molar specific heat at constant volume decreases by $\dfrac23R$ after this process ($R$ is universal gas constant). The mass of $\mathrm{O_2}$ in the mixture in grams is $M$. Find $M$. (Take : Degree of freedom of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ as 5)
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=single, subtopic={Mean free path}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: mean free path or collision frequency for a larger molecule | steps: collision cross section depends on diameter; mean free path scales; ratio}]
One mole of gas A, with molecular diameter $2d$ and average molecular speed $v$, is placed inside a certain container. Two moles of gas B, with molecular diameter $d$ and average molecular speed $2v$, is placed in an identical container. Ratio of average collision rate of gas A within its container to the average collision rate of gas B within its container is
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{1 : 3}
\opt{B}{1 : 1}
\opt{C}{3 : 1}
\opt{D}{2 : 1}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P1-PHY-S2-Q12, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=12, type=multi, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: diffusion rate, KMnO4 molecules through a tube from concentration difference | steps: partial pressure difference delta n k T; force on molecules; terminal drift speed relation with viscous drag; flux = n v S; compare with options}, also_in={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 02 (04 Feb 2021) P1 Q12}]
As shown schematically in the figure, two vessels contain water solutions (at temperature $T$) of potassium permanganate ($\mathrm{KMnO_4}$) of different concentrations $n_1$ and $n_2$ ($n_1>n_2$) molecules per unit volume with $\Delta n=(n_1-n_2)\ll n_1$. When they are connected by a tube of small length $\ell$ and cross-sectional area $S$, $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ starts to diffuse from the left to the right vessel through the tube. Consider the collection of molecules to behave as dilute ideal gases and the difference in their partial pressure in the two vessels causing the diffusion. The speed $v$ of the molecules is limited by the viscous force $-\beta v$ on each molecule, where $\beta$ is a constant. Neglecting all terms of the order $(\Delta n)^2$, which of the following is/are correct? ($k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant)-
\bfig{105.5}{SI11_p1_phy_s2_q12_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{the force causing the molecules to move across the tube is $\Delta n k_BTS$}
\opt{B}{force balance implies $n_1\beta v\ell=\Delta n k_BT$}
\opt{C}{total number of molecules going across the tube per sec is $\left(\dfrac{\Delta n}{\ell}\right)\left(\dfrac{k_BT}{\beta}\right)S$}
\opt{D}{rate of molecules getting transferred through the tube does not change with time}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI18-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={Score-I - Test 18 (24 Apr 2022)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Degrees of freedom}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: gas mixture of helium, nitrogen heated at constant volume and pressure | steps: Q = n Cv_mix dT and Q = n Cp_mix dT with dT 15 and 10; Cp - Cv = n R; solve moles and mixture heat capacities; ratio of moles of nitrogen and helium | I: mixture heat capacity is the mole weighted average}, also_in={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 01 (24 Jan 2021) P1 Q10}]
When heat $Q=600$ J is added to a mixture of helium and nitrogen at a constant volume the temperature of the mixture increases by 15 K and if the same amount of heat is given to the same mixture at constant pressure, the temperature of the mixture will increase by 10 K. Take $R=\dfrac{25}{3}$ Jmol k.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Ratio of number of nitrogen molecules and helium molecules in mixture is 1 : 1.}
\opt{B}{The internal energy changes more in isochoric process.}
\opt{C}{Work done by the gas is more in isobaric process.}
\opt{D}{The total number of moles in the mixture is 2.4 moles.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII03-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-II - Test 03 (05 May 2021)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S2 I0 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: gas samples with the same internal energy | steps: U = (f/2) n R T for each gas; hydrogen at 300 K has 5/2 R times 300; compare helium samples at the given temperatures}]

\opt{D}{2 mole of O$_2$ gas at 27$^\circ$C}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SII09-P2-PHY-S2-Q05, source={Score-II - Test 09 (12 Feb 2023)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I0 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: monatomic gas under a piston with a block, adiabatic process | steps: equilibrium pressure before and after; adiabatic compression of the gas; temperature ratio from P V relations; final state after removing the block}]

A block of mass 5 kg is put on top of piston and allowed to attain the equilibrium as in figure (b). The temperature of gas becomes $T_1$. After removing the block piston moves upward and when equilibrium is attained again temperature of gas becomes $T_2$. Neglect atmospheric pressure.
\bfig{213.9}{SII09_p2_phy_s2_q05_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$T_1=\dfrac53T_0$}
\opt{B}{$T_1=\dfrac73T_0$}
\opt{C}{$T_2=\dfrac54T_0$}
\opt{D}{$T_2=\dfrac74T_0$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SII12-P1-PHY-S4-Q04, source={Score-II - Test 12 (04 Feb 2024)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=numerical, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={308}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: effective gamma of a mixture of two ideal gases | steps: Cv of the mixture = (n1 Cv1 + n2 Cv2)/(n1+n2) from gamma values; gamma of the mixture; requested quantity such as the speed of sound or the ratio}]

The change in its internal energy is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Joule.

\begin{bankq}[id=SII12-P2-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-II - Test 12 (04 Feb 2024)}, paper=2, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={Degrees of freedom}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K2 S2 I0 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: degrees of freedom, internal energy and speed of sound | steps: U = n R T/2 grows with n; v = sqrt(gamma R T/M) with gamma = 1 + 2/n; compare}, also_in={Score-II - Test 40 (16 Mar 2025) P2 Q4}]
An ideal gas is in thermodynamic equilibrium. The number of degrees of freedom of a molecule of the gas in n. The internal energy of one mole of the gas is $U_n$ and the speed of sound in the gas is $v_n$. At a fixed temperature and pressure, which of the following is the correct option?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$v_3<v_6$ and $U_3>U_6$}
\opt{B}{$v_5>v_3$ and $U_3>U_5$}
\opt{C}{$v_5>v_7$ and $U_5<U_7$}
\opt{D}{$v_6<v_7$ and $U_6<U_7$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII25-P2-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-II - Test 25 (20 Mar 2024)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: speed of sound or gamma of a gas mixture | steps: mixture Cv from mole weighting; gamma mix; speed from molar mass average; statements | I: mixing rule for gamma and mean molar mass}]
A gas mixture contains $n_1$ mole of gas 1 (molar mass $M_1$) and $n_2$ mole of gas 2 (molar mass $M_2$) with adiabatic ratio $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ respectively with molar specific heats $C_{p_1}$, $C_{v_1}$ and $C_{p_2}$, $C_{v_2}$. Mixture is kept at temperature $T$ (in K) then choose the correct option.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Adiabatic ratio of mixture is $\gamma_{mix}=\dfrac{n_1\gamma_1+n_2\gamma_2}{n_1+n_2}$.}
\opt{B}{Adiabatic ratio of mixture is $\gamma_{mix}=\dfrac{n_1C_{p_1}+n_2C_{p_2}}{n_1C_{v_1}+n_2C_{v_2}}$.}
\opt{C}{rms speed of molecule in mixture $v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{\left(\frac{n_1M_1+n_2M_2}{n_1+n_2}\right)}}$.}
\opt{D}{rms speed of molecule in mixture $v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{\left(\frac{n_1+n_2}{\frac{n_1}{M_1}+\frac{n_2}{M_2}}\right)}}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=JA13-P2-PHY-S3-G1-2, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 13 (31 May 2021)}, questions={1-2}]
Let us consider a diatomic gas whose molecules have the shape of a dumbbell. In this model, the center of mass of the molecule can translate in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions. In addition, the molecule can rotate about three mutually perpendicular axes. We can neglect the rotation about the $y$-axis because the moment of inertia $I_y$ and the rotational energy $\frac12I_y\omega^2$ about this axis are negligible compared with those associated with the $x$ and $z$ axes. (If the two atoms are taken to be point masses, then $I_y$ is identically zero). Thus, there are five degrees of freedom: three associated with the translational motion and two associated with the rotational motion. Because each degree of freedom contributes, on the average, $\frac12k_BT$ of energy per molecule, the total internal energy for a system of $N$ molecules is:
\begin{gather*}E_{int}=3N\left(\tfrac12k_BT\right)+2N\left(\tfrac12k_BT\right)\\=\tfrac52Nk_BT=\tfrac52nRT\ \ldots\text{(i)}\end{gather*}
We can use this result to find the molar specific heat at constant volume:
\bfig{60.1}{JA13_p2_phy_s3_para1_2_1.png}
\[C_V=\frac1n\frac{dE_{int}}{dT}=\frac1n\frac d{dT}\left(\tfrac52nRT\right)=\tfrac52R\ \ldots\text{(ii)}\]
From equation (i) and (ii), we find that
\[C_P=C_V+R=\tfrac72R,\qquad \gamma=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=\frac{7/2R}{5/2R}=\frac75=1.40\]
In the vibratory model, the two atoms are joined by an imaginary spring. The vibrational motion adds two degrees of freedom, which correspond to the kinetic energy and the potential energy associated with vibrations along the length of the molecule about its centre of mass.
\end{bankpassage}
